# Torquing Strut Nut with Tire on Ground: The Physics of Vehicle Assembly

When you read a service manual instruction stating that strut mounting nuts should remain loose until the vehicle is on the ground, it often feels counterintuitive. In many other automotive contexts, such as wheel bearing preload or brake caliper alignment, components are tightened to spec while the assembly is suspended in the air. Leaving a critical fastener like the upper strut mount untorqued introduces an element of uncertainty that can seem risky if you aren't familiar with the underlying mechanics.

The reason for this procedure isn't arbitrary; it is dictated by how suspension geometry changes between static and dynamic states, specifically regarding weight transfer and camber gain. When a vehicle is hoisted on a lift or jack stands, the strut assembly carries no vertical load from the chassis to the wheel. The coil spring is compressed by its own initial preload, but the system is not under the full 1,500+ lbs of static axle weight plus dynamic forces that occur during braking and cornering.

If you tighten the top nut while the car is in the air, you are locking the strut tube into the mounting plate at a specific height relative to the knuckle. Once you lower the vehicle onto its tires, the suspension compresses under the full load of the car's mass. This compression causes the strut body to settle slightly deeper into the spring mount. If that top nut was already torqued to specification before this settlement occurred, two things happen: either the assembly cannot fully seat, preventing proper suspension travel, or more commonly, the torque value effectively increases as friction rises and metal deforms microscopically under load.

In many modern MacPherson strut designs, including those on a 2012 Subaru Outback, the upper mount includes a rubber isolator designed to dampen road noise and vibration. This isolator is pre-compressed by the assembly during installation. If you tighten the nut before lowering the car, you might crush this isolator beyond its intended range or prevent it from seating correctly against the tower top. A misaligned or improperly seated rubber mount can lead to premature wear, a persistent rattling noise under acceleration, or even catastrophic failure of the strut pivot ball due to uneven load distribution.

The correct workflow mimics a controlled release of potential energy. You install the new strut assembly, leave the top nut loose enough to allow free vertical movement of approximately 1/4 inch (or as specified in your specific manual), and then lower the vehicle completely. Only when the tires are firmly planted on the ground should you torque the upper strut mount nut to the manufacturer's specification. At this point, the suspension is under load, the geometry is settled into its resting position, and the rubber isolators are compressed exactly as they will be during normal operation.

Consider the torque value itself. A typical high-torque application for an Outback strut mount might range between 20 to 35 ft-lbs, depending on the specific year and trim. If you apply this force in a zero-G environment relative to the suspension load, you are essentially fighting only static friction and spring tension. By waiting until the car is grounded, you ensure that the bolt stretches uniformly against the actual forces it will encounter in service.

It is worth noting that while some manufacturers allow for "torque-to-yield" bolts or specific sequential tightening patterns, the fundamental rule of loading the suspension before final fastening remains consistent across most MacPherson strut architectures. Skipping this step might save you a few minutes of labor time, but it risks introducing alignment issues or structural fatigue later down the line. Always prioritize following the service manual's sequence over intuition when dealing with critical safety components like shock absorbers and struts.
